name: Lost in the Middle (Liu et al.)
publisher: Nelson F. Liu, Kevin Lin, John Hewitt, Ashwin Paranjape, Michele Bevilacqua, Fabio Petroni, Percy Liang (Stanford University, with co-authors from Samaya AI)
date_published: July 6, 2023 (arXiv v1, arXiv:2307.03172); later published in Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics (TACL), 2023/2024
claim_value: Across multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval tasks, model accuracy follows a U-shaped curve as a function of where the relevant information sits in the input: highest when it is at the very start (primacy) or very end (recency) of the context, and substantially lower, sometimes dropping below performance with no relevant document at all in some settings, when the relevant information is placed in the middle. This held across GPT-3.5-Turbo, several open models, and extended-context model variants; performance degraded even when total context length was well within the stated window limit.
claim_definition: An academic benchmark finding: controlled position-manipulation experiments (moving the one relevant document to different indices within a fixed-length, multi-document context) measuring QA/retrieval accuracy as a function of position, isolating a positional-bias effect distinct from pure length effects.
reproducibility: Code and data are public (Stanford NLP group released the evaluation code and data alongside the paper; the arXiv PDF and project materials are openly available at cs.stanford.edu/~nfliu). The finding has been widely replicated and extended by independent follow-up work, not just cited: 'Found in the Middle' (2024) studies and attempts to calibrate the same positional-attention bias, and multiple long-context benchmark papers (including NoLiMa, 2025) explicitly reproduce or build on the lost-in-the-middle phenomenon in new model generations. This is a well-replicated academic result, unlike the single-publisher Chroma report.
publisher_sells_relevant_product: No. Authors are Stanford University researchers (with two co-authors affiliated with Samaya AI, a search/retrieval startup at the time); Samaya AI's retrieval focus is a mild adjacency, but the paper is an academic publication in a peer-reviewed venue (TACL), not vendor marketing, and the paper's framing is diagnostic rather than promotional.
conflict_notes: No numeric discrepancy found between the primary arXiv/TACL paper and how it is commonly cited in secondary sources reviewed in this pass (inblog.ai, Substack explainers, lecture slides all describe the U-shaped curve and the beginning/end-versus-middle contrast consistently with the primary text). [uncertain]
relationship: Supports the technical case for context engineering by establishing, well before the 'context engineering' label existed, that simply having relevant information somewhere in the context window is not sufficient; position matters independently of whether the model 'knows' the fact. This underpins practices like reordering or re-ranking retrieved chunks so key evidence lands near the start or end of the prompt. It does not address prompt wording/instruction quality at all, so it neither supports nor contradicts 'prompt engineering is dead'; it is orthogonal to that claim and is sometimes misapplied as if it settled it.
derivative_of: Not derivative; this is treated by later work (Context Rot, NoLiMa, 'Found in the Middle', and general context-engineering commentary) as the foundational empirical result they extend, confirm, or complicate, rather than something it itself repackages. It builds methodologically on earlier needle-in-a-haystack-style long-context probes but is the first widely-cited paper to isolate and name the positional U-curve specifically.
register: academic researcher primarily, with heavy secondary uptake by practitioner/engineer audiences (it is the most frequently cited academic paper in practitioner context-engineering blog posts) and some enterprise-IT-buyer secondary citation as justification for retrieval re-ranking products.
notes: Later work complicates the original framing in one specific way worth flagging: NoLiMa (2025) found that when literal lexical overlap between question and answer is removed, degradation is not confined to the middle position, it becomes severe across all positions at longer lengths, suggesting the clean U-shape partly depended on the easier literal-matching retrieval setup Liu et al. used. So the phenomenon is confirmed as real but the original paper's tidy middle-is-worst geometry is less universal once lexical shortcuts are removed. [uncertain]
already_cited: No. article_ideas.md's 'Context engineering didn't retire the prompt' entry (2026-09-27) does not name this paper, Liu et al., Stanford, or the lost-in-the-middle finding; it cites an unnamed 2026 industry survey instead. No other article_ideas.md or AGENTS.md entry reviewed in this pass names it either.
new_angle: Supplies the missing academic backbone under the existing thought: where the logged entry currently argues from an opinion survey (82% of leaders), this paper gives a mechanistic, peer-reviewed, independently-replicated reason why 'put it in context' isn't enough, which is a stronger foundation than a survey stat. It also supplies a built-in complication (via NoLiMa) that keeps the piece honest: the tidy 'middle is bad' story softens once you remove literal keyword overlap, so the piece can avoid overclaiming the geometry while still using the core positional-sensitivity finding.
